opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I have somewhat complicated feelings about this. I'll start with the part where I'm skeptical and then get to the part where I think it's reasonable.

The skeptical part comes from the adversarial examples literature. For years people proposed detectors: "We can't make the classifier robust, but we can detect when an input is adversarial and reject it." Then people would stack them: one detector looks at this statistic, another at that one, and surely an attacker can't fool all of them at once. Over and over, that turned out to be false. If the attacker knows what you're doing, fooling three detectors is usually not much harder than fooling one. You just add the terms to the loss function and optimize against all of them together. The layers aren't independent in the way the defender hopes. The intuition people have, that if each layer catches 90 percent then three layers catch 99.9 percent, assumes failures are independent, and against an adaptive adversary they almost never are. The attacker finds the input that slips through everything at once.

So when I hear "defense in depth with layered detectors" for language models, my first reaction is: have you evaluated it against someone who is actually trying to break the whole stack, not each piece separately?

Now the part where I'm more sympathetic. In traditional computer security, defense in depth is completely correct, and the reason is that it changes the economics. You're not claiming any layer is perfect. You're making the attack more expensive, more fragile, more likely to get noticed. If you're running a deployed system where you can watch traffic, ban accounts, and patch things, then a detector that an attacker *can* evade but has to work at evading is genuinely valuable. Most attackers are not sophisticated. Raising the bar filters out a lot of them, and the ones who remain leave traces.

So I think it's a fine approach as long as you're honest about what you're claiming. If you say "this makes misuse harder and gives us monitoring signal," great, I believe that. If you say "this makes the system secure against a determined adversary," I don't believe that, and I'd want to see a serious adaptive attack evaluation before I did.

The thing I worry about most is people using the layered setup as a reason to stop working on the hard problem. It's tempting: the underlying model isn't robust, but we've wrapped it in enough filters that it seems fine on the benchmarks. Then someone who cares enough shows up and it falls over. For the threat models where that matters a lot, the really high-stakes ones, I don't think detectors save you. For everyday abuse prevention, they're probably one of the more practical tools we have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses layered detectors but does not mention block ciphers or confusion and diffusion.

r002.rationale: It endorses layers for raising attack costs and monitoring, but does not frame them as an empirically effective fallback when no principled account of robustness is available.

r003.rationale: It says an adaptive attacker can find an input that slips through the whole stack, but does not identify a fundamentally different attack as the way this could happen.

r004.rationale: It calls detectors practical for everyday abuse prevention, but does not present them as a fallback if full robustness proves unattainable.

r005.rationale: The response endorses detectors for practical use, but does not say they remain useful even if robust AI systems are achievable.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that defense in depth is a phrase that sounds much better than it usually turns out to be in practice, and I want to be careful about why.

The intuition people have is something like: I have detector A that catches 90% of attacks, detector B that catches 90% of attacks, so if I stack them I catch 99%. And that math only works if the failures are independent. In the adversarial setting they are almost never independent, because the adversary isn't sampling attacks at random from some distribution and hoping. The adversary is optimizing. They get to look at the whole system and find the single input that slips past all of your layers simultaneously. So the right mental model isn't that the layers multiply the attacker's difficulty, it's that the attacker's job is now to find the intersection of all the holes, and that intersection is usually still quite large.

We saw this very concretely in the adversarial examples literature. Around 2017, 2018, there was a wave of papers proposing detection methods for adversarial examples, and almost every one evaluated against attacks that didn't know the detector existed. When you actually write the attack to target the detector as well as the classifier, essentially all of them fell over, often with very little additional cost to the attacker. I spent a fair amount of time breaking those, and the pattern repeated so reliably that I became pretty skeptical of any claim that depends on the attacker not adapting.

Now, that's the critique. I don't think the conclusion is that layering is useless. There are a couple of places where it does buy you something real.

One is against non-adaptive or low-effort adversaries, which, frankly, is most of the traffic most systems see. If your threat model is someone copying a jailbreak off of a forum, a second independent filter genuinely helps, because that person isn't going to iterate against your specific stack. You just have to be honest that this is the threat you're defending against, and not claim you've solved the problem for a motivated attacker.

Two is when the layers are actually mechanistically different. If detector A and detector B are both neural networks trained on roughly similar data, they tend to share blind spots, and an input that fools one is suspiciously likely to fool the other. If one layer is a learned classifier and another is a rate limit, or a sandbox, or a human in the loop for high-stakes actions, those fail for different reasons, and that's where the independence assumption starts to hold a little bit. The things that matter most in practice tend to be the boring systems-security controls, not the extra ML model bolted on the front.

The thing I'd really push on is evaluation. If someone shows me a layered system, the question I want answered is: did you give the attacker white-box access to every layer and let them optimize against all of it at once? If the answer is no, I don't think you've learned very much about how robust it is. And this is uncomfortable, because the whole appeal of defense in depth is that it feels like it should let you avoid that hard question. It doesn't. It just moves it.

So my assessment is something like: it's a reasonable engineering practice, it raises the floor against unsophisticated attackers, and it should never be mistaken for a solution to adversarial robustness. The security community learned this lesson decades ago with things like stacking antivirus signatures, and I think the machine learning community is relearning it with a slight lag.

r002.rationale: It says layering can help against non-adaptive attackers, but does not present empirically effective layered defenses as a fallback when no principled explanation of robustness is available.

r003.rationale: It explains that an adaptive attacker can optimize against the whole system and find an input that slips past all layers simultaneously.

r004.rationale: The response calls layering a reasonable engineering practice and says it raises the floor, but does not identify layered detectors as a fallback if full robustness proves unattainable.

r005.rationale: The response describes situations where layered defenses help, but does not state that detectors remain useful even if robust AI systems are achievable.

astra-6.text:
I think defense in depth is a good principle, but you have to be careful about what you’re counting as an independent layer of defense. If you have five detectors that all make essentially the same mistakes, you don’t necessarily get much more security than you had with one detector.

The tempting argument is: each detector catches 90 percent of attacks, so if I stack several of them, the probability of getting through becomes tiny. But that only works under assumptions about independence that you really need to justify. An attacker isn’t randomly sampling attacks from the distribution you evaluated. They’re looking for the particular thing that gets through your entire system.

So the experiment I want to see is an adaptive attack against the whole stack. Give the attacker knowledge of the defenses, let them develop an attack that accounts for those defenses, and then measure how well the system holds up. Testing each component separately and multiplying the success rates doesn’t establish that.

That doesn’t mean detectors are useless. They can raise the cost of an attack, and that can be valuable. But I’d feel much better about layers that enforce different kinds of constraints—for example, a detector combined with a sandbox and limited permissions—than several models all being asked whether the same input looks malicious. Then a mistake in the detector doesn’t automatically give the attacker the ability to do something consequential.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention block ciphers or confusion and diffusion.

r002.rationale: It says detectors can raise attack costs, but does not present empirically effective layered defenses as a fallback when no principled robustness explanation is available.

r003.rationale: It describes an adaptive attacker developing an attack that accounts for the defenses and tests whether it can get through the whole stack.

r004.rationale: The response discusses layered detectors as useful, but does not frame them as a fallback if full robustness proves unattainable.

r005.rationale: It says detectors remain useful, but does not connect that claim to robust AI systems being achievable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think defense in depth is a good principle, but the important question is whether the layers fail independently. If you put five detectors in front of a model, and they all detect essentially the same kinds of things, you may have five components without getting much additional security. An attacker who finds a way around one might find that the same attack gets around all five.

And you have to evaluate the whole system against an attacker who knows those layers exist. You can’t just measure each detector separately and multiply the failure probabilities. That assumes exactly the independence you need to demonstrate.

What I’d want is layers that do different things: a detector that catches some attacks, restrictions on what the model can access, and limits on what actions it can take even if an attack succeeds. Then a detector failure doesn’t automatically become a catastrophic failure. Detectors can be useful, but I’d be much more comfortable if the security of the system didn’t depend on them catching everything.
